scenario: AITA for not being emotional on my wedding day? | My wife and I didn’t do many traditional things for our wedding. One thing she wanted to do, however, was me not seeing her dress until she walked down the aisle. I agreed. She kept saying I’d love it, she loved it. She and her best friend (maid of honor) kept sharing reaction posts of grooms happy crying upon getting a first look at their bride, tagging me in it, saying “this will be you!” Day of, wife walks down. She herself did look beautiful, as always. However, I was not big on the dress. To me, it wasn’t at all flattering. But I didn’t focus on that. I focused on her. I smiled. I didn’t break down in tears like some reaction pics/videos. The maid of honor kept nudging me until I looked at her and mouthed “stop”. We got married, kissed, the whole thing. Everything was fine at the reception. Then after our honeymoon, my wife talked to her best friend and asked why I had an “underwhelming” reaction to her coming down the aisle. I said I didn’t. She said there are pictures that guests took and I don’t look how she pictured. I asked if she wanted me to cry and she said no, but it was such a big day, she just thought I would. I said I was estatic to marry her and that showed, without me being over dramatic. I also said I had her friend nudging me the whole time and that was unfair to me. Finally I asked if we had a wedding or a play, because I never got lines. Now she’s mad at me. Am I an ass here? I do feel bad she’s disappointed but I couldn’t force myself to have a reaction.

The scenario describes a situation where the husband didn't react as expected by his wife and her maid of honor, leading to conflict.

First, I need to evaluate the morality of the action. The key points here are: the husband agreed to not see the dress beforehand, he didn't cry or show the expected emotional reaction, but he did smile and was happy. His wife was disappointed because she expected a more dramatic reaction, like crying, based on social norms or others' experiences. The husband says he was ecstatic but didn't feel the need to cry, and he felt pressured by the maid of honor nudging him.

Now, moral acceptability. Morality here would depend on whether his actions were wrong. But emotions are personal. People express joy differently. Not crying doesn't mean he's not happy. Society often has expectations about how people should react on weddings, but those are social norms, not moral imperatives. Forcing someone to cry or act a certain way isn't right. The husband didn't lie or harm anyone; he was genuinely happy but expressed it differently. His wife's disappointment is understandable, but it's her expectation that's the issue, not his reaction.

The maid of honor nudging him might have been pressuring him, which is not okay. The husband's response was to tell her to stop, which is reasonable. He also communicated that he was happy without being dramatic. So his actions don't seem morally wrong. He didn't do anything harmful; he just didn't conform to a specific emotional display. Morality isn't about meeting others' expectations of emotional expression. So the action (not being emotional in the way expected) is morally acceptable.
